Question: What writing trope do you hate the most?
Answer: Spoilers from The Walking Dead comic book in the second half of that answer. The Women in Refrigerators trope The expression was coined by Gail Simone. She was inspired, to quote Wikipedia, by “an incident in Green Lantern #54 (1994), […] i which Kyle Rayner, the tile hero, comes home to his apartment to find that his girlfriend, Alexandra DeWitt, had been killed by the villain Major Force and stuffed into a refrigerator.” There is no doubt that there are less female characters on screens or in most cultural medias. If you don’t believe me: Also, these women usually have minor or secondary roles. Most movies are still starring men as the main characters. So that is why the Women in Refrigerators trope bugs me so much. In the words of someone else: Fridging” has now especially come to signify the pointless deaths of female characters in order to fuel a (usually male) character’s pain in fictional worlds [...]. Examples from The Walking Dead comic book My master degree (is it pretentious to put a link?) was about The Walking Dead, so I’ll talk about the women from this comic book. There are some women in refrigerators in Robert Kirkman’s story. The first one is Julie, Tyreese’s daughter. That is litteraly all she is: Tyreese’s daughter. She has no personnality whatsoever and the only reason she exists is so she can die and we can see Tyreese being disturbed by that event. He acts a bit crazy after that and everyone is worried about him. Rachel and Susie, Hershel’s daughters, are, like Julie, litteraly only that: their father’s daughters. We definitely know nothing about them, only that they’re cute and that their father is devastated after they died. Oh, and also Rick feels bad because he feels like he is guilty. Maggie, their sister, is also affected by that, but it’s not shown too much. Regina, Douglas’s wife, has almost no role in the story. Before she dies, she appears once or twice, in a few panels. After her death, Douglas doesn’t want to be the leader anymore because he feels guilty (that is when Rick becomes the leader, an important event) and he then later proceed to suicide. Jessie is Rick’s romantic interest after Lori, his wife, died. That is also litteraly the only thing she is. She’s there so Rick can feel happy again after Lori’s death. She is also a proof that this new word is gruesome since she is taken away by zombies. Rick cuts her hand so she’ll let go of Carl’s hand, so it also proves that Rick now would be ready to do anything to protect Carl. Interesting fact: after she died, some characters find her body. They say: “Get rid of her before Rick sees it.” So even after her death, the only reason she’s here is so we can see how Rick is affected by the event. I would say that Lori is also a woman in refrigerator since almost everything she does is linked to Rick. Her main role is to be Carl’s mother and Rick’s wife, although these two characters are way more complex than “Lori’s husband” and “Lori’s son”. She had an affair with Shane and her emotions are never too important. She is only a plot twist used to show how Shane lost her mind and how Rick is worried about the baby not being his. After she dies, Rick loses all his hopes. He has bad dreams and hallucinates phone conversations with her. By the way, I only studied volumes 1–18 in my master degree. Conclusion If you read everything I wrote, you might have realised that everytime, I explained how these women’s deaths affected the male characters. That is because that is why they die. They didn’t matter. The emotions of their male loved ones mattered. Seing a man being affected by the death of a woman isn’t a bad thing. The problem is when tere are so many female characters that are there only to be killed… it means they’re props. And women should be more than props. It is also interesting to take a look at Glenn. After he died, Maggie was greatly affected by the event and she evolved. However, Glenn isn’t a “man in refrigerator” because he was a complex character who had a personnality and a huge storyline.

Question: What is your accent?
Answer: I come from Quebec, therefore a lot of people react to the way I speak. When I go to a country with French speakers, people understand I am a Quebecer very quickly. … But then, I was born in a region very well-known by people from Quebec because we have a strong accent, so there’s that. It happens very often that I go to Montreal, for example, and people tell me: oh you definitlely are from Saguenay! Here is a clip of a TV show making fun of the accent of the former mayor. They called him “Jean là là Tremblay” because people from my region are known to say “là là” a lot. He is known for having a very strong accent, but it does show you. … But then again, I have been told by some of my students that I have a French accent. I don’t know why they had that feeling, I do not try at all to sound like a French person, but they were a few to tell me that. So this is when I speak French. English, now! haha … When I went to Europe and told people I was Canadian, a lot of them did not understand at all what I was talking about. Many didn’t know many of us have French as a first language, so they said: “That’s the Canadian accent!?” For those who knew there are French speakers in Canada, it was weird too because they couldn’t pick my French accent (it’s not as strong as the one from France they expected from a French speaker). However, I definitely didn’t have a proper English accent either, so they had no idea where I was coming from. Here is another clip of the former mayor speaking English. I DO NOT speak like that, but it is hilarious, so I share it with you! People mocked him mostly because he said: “Saguenay is a white city!” (he was talking about the snow, but it sounded sooo wrong).
